title: Run result document
description:
The engine's OUTPUT contract: what the platform renders after a run. Normative. `sample-result-batch.json` and `sample-result-single-api.json` are illustrative only.

A result document is written on EVERY path, ABORTED included, so a consumer never has to special-case 'nothing came back'. The ABORTED document validates against this same schema - every key a consumer reads is present, all seven counts at zero and `cleanBlockers` an empty array, rather than `counts: {}` and no `cleanBlockers` at all. That drift had already shipped one KeyError, on the one code path least able to retry.

THE TWO RULES THAT MATTER MOST:
  1. RUN STATUS IS ORTHOGONAL TO TEST OUTCOMES. A test FAIL is not a run failure. `COMPLETED` means every requested tier executed, however many assertions failed. Never wire a UI to the process exit code - read `status`.
  2. PASS RATE IS `PASS / (PASS + FAIL)`. NOTHING ELSE. The other five states stay out of the denominator and stay individually countable. `passRate` is `null` when the denominator is zero; render that as 'not applicable', NEVER as 100%.

runId.description: Echoed from the manifest, so a run is identifiable from its output. `"unknown"` when a run aborted before a manifest could be read.

environment.description: The normalized environment the run targeted. Empty string on an ABORTED run that never got as far as reading one.

requestedTiers.description: Echoed from the manifest. Empty array on an ABORTED run that never read one.

catalogueVersion.description: The catalogue version these results join against. Join on the IDs, never on position.

statusReason.description:
Why the run is not plainly `COMPLETED`, or `""` when it is.

EMPTY IS MEANINGFUL. A wrong `authProviderApiId` produces `COMPLETED` with `statusReason: ""` and ordinary FAILs - the bootstrap succeeded and the token was rejected in use, so nothing at run level went wrong. Do not read an empty reason as 'nothing to see'; read the per-API `gatewayClassification`.

applicabilityNote.description:
Prose restating the one legal applicability transition: a test the catalogue predicted `PLANNED` may report `NOT_APPLICABLE` at run time, and the reverse cannot happen.

OPTIONAL - and this is not an oversight. The ABORTED document omits it, because a run that never started has no applicability to describe. Read it defensively.

summary.description: The whole run, aggregated. Computed from the same records as the per-API summaries, never recomputed from them.

apis.description: One report per API. EMPTY on an ABORTED run - that is the normal shape of 'nothing ran', not a malformed document.

runStatus.description:
RUN-level status only, deliberately independent of individual test outcomes.

  COMPLETED             - every requested tier executed. Exit 0. Tests may still have failed.
  COMPLETED_WITH_ERRORS - a tier ran only partially: some APIs never executed because their auth
                          bootstrap failed. Exit 0 - THE RUN HAPPENED, the APIs were blocked.
                          Individual test failures never reach this state.
  ABORTED               - a tier could not start. Exit 2. No tests ran; `apis` is empty.

Exit 3 means the runner itself broke, and emits an ABORTED document.

Read `status` from the document, never the exit code, to tell a failing test from a failing run.

resultState.description:
The seven states every contract check resolves to exactly one of:

  PASS             - assertion ran and succeeded.
  FAIL             - assertion ran and failed.
  WARN             - ran; an advisory threshold was exceeded; the run is NOT failed.
  SKIPPED_NO_TOKEN - auth bootstrap failed, so the API was never executed.
  NOT_APPLICABLE   - the check cannot apply because required metadata is absent.
  NOT_ASSERTED     - the request executed but no assertion exists for it.
  INFORMATIONAL    - observes and records; asserts nothing about the response.

PASS and FAIL are the ONLY two that may appear in a pass-rate denominator. Collapsing the other five into 'skipped', or worse into 'passed', is what this vocabulary exists to prevent: most requests in the source collections carry no assertions at all, and rendering those green would make the headline number a lie on day one.

gatewayClassification.description:
Why a request was rejected, when the status code alone cannot say.

  AUTH_FAILURE_401             - the application rejected the token.
  APPLICATION_AUTH_FAILURE_403 - the application refused the request.
  GATEWAY_WAF_EMPTY_BODY_403   - THE REQUEST NEVER REACHED THE APPLICATION.

The third is an empty-bodied 403 with `content-length: 0` and a non-JSON content type - a WAF/gateway block. Rendering it as 'your API failed' would be wrong for an entire module. Say 'blocked by gateway' instead.

The first is also the signal that distinguishes a mis-pointed `authProviderApiId` from a genuinely broken endpoint: when several FAILs on one API all cite 401 and the API carries this classification, suspect the provider before filing a bug.

total.description: Countable results - results that merely reference a host measurement carried by another API are excluded. See `referencedHostResults`.

referencedHostResults.description:
How many results were dropped from the tally because they reference a host-level measurement another API carried.

A host-level probe runs ONCE PER HOST. Counting the other APIs behind that host as separate results would inflate the neighbours of the denominator and make a batch look far more skipped than it is - 45 APIs behind 3 hosts is 3 measurements, not 45.

passRate.description:
`PASS / (PASS + FAIL)`, rounded to 4 decimal places. NOTHING ELSE goes in the denominator.

`null` means NOT APPLICABLE - the denominator was zero, so no pass rate exists. A batch of entirely unasserted APIs has no pass rate. RENDER `null` AS 'not applicable'; reporting it as 100% is the exact failure this whole design exists to prevent. `passRateApplicable` says the same thing as a boolean for consumers that cannot easily test for null.

passRateBasis.description: The formula, published in the document so a consumer never re-derives it and gets it wrong. Constant by contract.

clean.description:
True only when nothing needs a human to look at it: no blocking state present AND a pass rate exists. One WARN or one blocked API is not a clean pass.

`clean: false` beside `passRate: 1.0` is NOT a contradiction and NOT an engine bug - every assertion really did pass, and a WARN or a blocked API is still waiting on someone. `cleanBlockers` says which.

cleanBlockers.description:
Which blocking states are actually present, WORST FIRST - element zero is the headline cause. Derived from the same counts as `clean`, so the two can never disagree.

Only these three states block: FAIL, WARN, SKIPPED_NO_TOKEN.

EMPTY WHILE `clean` IS FALSE means exactly one thing: no blocking state is present and the pass rate is inapplicable - nothing landed in PASS + FAIL at all. `passRateApplicable` already says so, which is why this stays strictly a list of states.

REQUIRED ON EVERY PATH, including ABORTED, where it is `[]`.

counts.title: Per-state tally
counts.description: ALL SEVEN STATES ARE ALWAYS PRESENT, ZEROED RATHER THAN ABSENT - including on an ABORTED run. A consumer reading `counts["FAIL"]` must never have to guard for a missing key.

provenance.title: Where this API came from
provenance.description: Empty object where the engine had nothing to record. Open to additional keys on purpose - provenance is descriptive metadata, and a new source type must not invalidate an otherwise-good document.

sourceCollection.description: The file the API was read from, repo-relative.

owner.description: Null rather than back-filled with a guess.

apiRef.description: Identifies the API these results belong to. For an inventory API this is the manifest `ref`; for an uploaded definition it is a derived identifier that includes the base URL.

gatewayClassification.description: Always present at API level, `null` when no auth-shaped rejection was seen. Check this before filing a bug against an endpoint whose FAILs all cite 401.

result.title: One test outcome for one API
result.description: Seven keys are always present. The rest appear conditionally, and the conditions are enforced below: a NOT_APPLICABLE result always carries `missingField`, a WARN always carries both numbers, a SKIPPED_NO_TOKEN always carries `blockedBy`, and a host-level result always carries all four host keys.

testId.description: Joins to the catalogue's `testCases`. Deterministic and free of run-specific data. Global and generated IDs derive from code identifiers and survive any title change; Newman IDs are title-derived and do NOT - renaming a `pm.test()` string retires one case and introduces another.

apiRef.description: Repeated from the enclosing API report so a flattened result row stands alone.

reason.description:
Human-readable detail, with the machine-readable markers already stripped out. May be empty for a plain PASS.

NEVER CLASSIFY ON PROSE, and never on the underlying pytest verdict: WARN and INFORMATIONAL are emitted as pytest skips because that is the only built-in non-failing outcome carrying a machine-readable reason, but BOTH MEAN THE CHECK RAN. Read `state`, and `executed`.

durationMs.description: Wall-clock for this check, to 3 decimal places. `0` for a check that never executed.

executed.description:
Whether the check actually ran against the API. True for PASS, FAIL, WARN and INFORMATIONAL; false for the other three.

WARN and INFORMATIONAL are true here despite surfacing as pytest skips. Treating them as 'did not execute' understates real coverage.

missingField.description:
REQUIRED WHEN `state` IS `NOT_APPLICABLE`, absent otherwise. Names the metadata field whose absence disabled the check, so a consumer can say 'declare this' instead of 'something is missing'.

NULLABLE, AND `null` IS NOT A DEGRADED VALUE - it means NOTHING IS MISSING. The opt-in CORS preflight check is the standing example: it reports NOT_APPLICABLE because it is switched off, not because the definition lacks anything, so `missingField` is `null`. DO NOT RENDER A `null` HERE AS A METADATA GAP.

observed.description: REQUIRED WHEN `state` IS `WARN`. The measured value. A WARN is only actionable with both numbers, so the threshold is never left implicit.

threshold.description: REQUIRED WHEN `state` IS `WARN`. The advisory target that was exceeded.

blockedBy.description:
REQUIRED WHEN `state` IS `SKIPPED_NO_TOKEN`, absent otherwise. The `authProviderApiId` whose bootstrap failed - naming what to go and fix is what makes a blocked API actionable.

`null` where nothing named a provider: a check that needed a bearer token when the session never bootstrapped one. Null rather than inventing a provider that did not fail.

hostLevel.description: Present and true only on a host-level probe - a check measuring a HOST or GATEWAY property rather than an endpoint property. Absent entirely on ordinary results.

host.description: Which host was measured. Present on every host-level result.

referencesHostResult.description:
True when this API is REFERENCING a measurement another API carried, rather than having measured it itself. Referencing rows are excluded from `summary.total` and from the counts.

Deliberately NOT the same question as `measuredBy != apiRef`: a host-level row blocked by auth before the dedup check ever ran is a genuine SKIPPED_NO_TOKEN and must stay counted, even though another API carries its host measurement.

measuredBy.description:
The `apiRef` that actually carried this host measurement - THIS ROW'S OWN REF WHEN IT IS THE ONE THAT MEASURED. Populated on every host-level result, self included, so a consumer never has to special-case 'this row did its own measuring'.

FOLLOW THIS BEFORE READING A HOST-LEVEL `NOT_APPLICABLE` AS A GAP: it usually means the probe ran once elsewhere on the same host, not that anything is missing.

gatewayClassification.description: Present on a result only when an auth-shaped rejection was classified. Absent otherwise - at result level this key is omitted rather than nulled.

allOf.$comment: NOT_APPLICABLE must name the gap, or explicitly say there isn't one.
A WARN carries both numbers so the threshold is never implicit.
A blocked API is actionable only once you know which credential to fix.
A host-level result carries all four host keys or none of them.
